name: Bench press

lead: The bench press is a weight-training exercise in which the lifter lies on a bench and presses a weight upward. It mainly works the pectoralis major, with the front shoulders and triceps assisting, and is one of the standard chest-building lifts in bodybuilding and general training.

For looks, a larger chest, shoulders and triceps contribute to a broader, more muscular upper body. The press is also one of the three powerlifting events, so strength on it is widely tracked and discussed, including on looksmaxxing forums.

paras: Lifters use a barbell or dumbbells on a flat, incline or decline bench, with variations in grip width and bench angle that shift emphasis between chest and triceps. Programs place it in split routines or full-body routines, with protein intake, rest and progressive loading discussed as supporting factors. Visible chest growth takes months of consistent training.

Reported injuries include rotator cuff and pectoral tears, distal clavicle bone erosion and, rarely, neck or spine problems; being pinned under the bar is a hazard when lifting alone, which dumbbells and safety arms reduce. Research has measured shoulder load differences between technique variations.

angle.text: The press trains the chest, front delts and triceps, and repeated progressive loading adds muscle in those areas. Lifters use it as a core upper-body size and strength lift.

lead: The bench press is a weight-training exercise performed lying on a bench, pressing a barbell or pair of dumbbells upward from the chest to full arm extension. Its main working muscle is the pectoralis major, with the anterior deltoids and triceps assisting and the serratus anterior, trapezius, rotator cuff and core acting as stabilisers.[1] It is one of the three lifts contested in powerlifting, alongside the squat and deadlift, and one of the most widely performed chest exercises in gyms.[1][2]

People use it to improve how their upper body looks. Progressive loading of the press adds muscle to the chest, front shoulders and triceps, which contributes to a fuller chest and broader-looking torso. Grip width and bench angle change which muscles take most of the work: a wider grip emphasises the pectorals, a narrower grip the triceps, and incline benches shift emphasis toward the upper chest and front deltoids.[1][3][2]

The lift has a long history in strength sport, a large body of training research on volume, frequency, rest periods and supplements, and an established list of recognised injuries. In looksmaxxing communities it appears mainly as a benchmark for gym progress and in debates about chest development, with members posting numbers such as one-rep maxes and plate milestones.[4][5]

paras: In the standard version the lifter lies on a flat bench, grips a barbell at about shoulder width or wider, retracts the shoulder blades, lowers the bar to the middle or lower sternum and presses until the elbows lock out, with the feet planted on the floor.[1] The primary movers are the pectoralis major, anterior deltoids and triceps brachii; the anconeus assists elbow extension and the pectoralis minor is active in flat pressing, while the serratus anterior, trapezius, rotator cuff and core stabilise.[1]

Biomechanical descriptions in reference summaries mention a slight J-shaped bar path, elbows at roughly 45 to 75 degrees from the torso, and leg drive transferring force through the body.[2] Because these figures come from an AI-generated encyclopedia summary, they are best read as general coaching conventions rather than measured findings.

In competition the head, shoulders and glutes must stay on the bench, the feet must stay flat, and the bar must pause on the chest until the referee signals the press; at the bottom, rules in some federations require the elbows to be level with or below the shoulders. Rules vary between federations.[1] Arching the back and deep breathing are common competition techniques, and Wikipedia notes that very large arches have been criticised for shortening the range of motion.[1]

Common variants include incline and decline presses, close-grip and wide-grip presses, board presses for partial-range work, floor presses, dumbbell presses, Smith-machine and selectorised chest-press machines, and related movements such as dips and push-ups.[2] Dumbbells allow a greater range of motion and unilateral work, and Wikipedia notes they can be dropped safely and allow more external rotation at the shoulder.[1][2] A published study that compared bench angles measured how muscular activation in the upper extremity changed with the angle of the bench.[3]

Early lifters mostly used the strict floor press. Wikipedia reports that George Hackenschmidt performed a strict floor press of 164 kg in 1899, a mark that stood until Joe Nordquest exceeded it by one kilogram in 1916, and that lifters of that period began using an explosive glute bridge to drive the bar from the abdomen to lockout.[1]

The bench press grew popular from the late 1950s, overtaking the parallel dip as the standard chest exercise even though the dip needs no spotter or safety bars.[1] An AI-generated reference summary adds that the Amateur Athletic Union treated it as one of the big three lifts in the 1960s and that the International Powerlifting Federation was founded in 1972, though these details were not independently checked.[2]

The NFL Scouting Combine uses the bench press as a test of upper-body muscular endurance, with prospects performing as many repetitions as possible at 225 lb (102 kg).[1] That weight became a widely quoted gym milestone, the 225 club, which lifters on forums such as T Nation also use as a reference point.[2][6]

Wikipedia lists the men's raw bench press record as 355 kg (783 lb), held by Julius Maddox, and the equipped (bench shirt) record as 635 kg (1,400 lb), held by Jimmy Kolb; it credits the rise from 164 kg to these figures over roughly a century to improved technique, training and drug use.[1] Another reference summary gives Maddox's lift as set on 21 February 2021 under the WRPF and lists a raw women's record of 207.5 kg.[2] Equipped records use supportive shirts and differ from raw lifts, and records vary by federation and weight class.[1][2]

The press is a standard component of bodybuilding and general physique routines because it loads the chest, shoulders and triceps heavily and allows progressive increases in weight. Programs place it in split routines, such as push days, or in full-body routines. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies and 392 participants found similar changes in bench press strength and in cross-sectional area of the elbow extensors and flexors after split and full-body routines.[7] A separate randomized trial also compared the two approaches.[8]

Proponents of heavy barbell pressing argue that it is the most direct way to thicken the chest, and some lifters add incline and dumbbell work for the upper chest. A T Nation forum member described a routine of Hammer Strength incline presses, flies, dumbbell presses and dips over about half a year that, in his words, brought up his pecs.[9] Another T Nation contributor mentioned dropping bench variations altogether and training the chest less directly.[10] Both views appear in lifting communities.

Much of the research on strength and size relevant to the bench press examines general resistance-training variables. A randomized trial of 34 resistance-trained men compared low-, moderate- and high-volume training and found that higher volume increased muscle hypertrophy but not strength.[11] A systematic review and meta-analysis of the minimum effective dose for increasing one-rep-max strength included the bench press among the powerlifts it considered.[12] A trial in resistance-trained men found that longer rest periods between sets improved strength and hypertrophy.[13] A narrative review on time-efficient programs recommends including a bilateral upper-body pushing exercise such as the bench press, at least four weekly sets per muscle group, and notes that weekly volume matters more than frequency.[14]

A 2025 randomized trial in 42 young resistance-trained men and women compared single-set training to failure with training stopped two repetitions short, measuring muscular adaptations.[15] Researchers have also studied how strength training affects shoulder proprioception.[16]

A meta-analysis of 74 randomized trials found that increasing daily protein intake was associated with greater lean body mass gains in studies of people doing resistance exercise (standardised mean difference 0.22).[17] A 2025 meta-analysis of 69 studies reported that creatine plus resistance training produced small but statistically significant improvements in bench and chest press strength (weighted mean difference 1.43 kg).[18] A meta-analysis of magnesium supplementation examined muscle fitness outcomes including bench press weights.[19]

A 1996 New England Journal of Medicine trial gave supraphysiologic testosterone doses to normal men and reported increased muscle size and strength, with the largest gains in men who also exercised.[20] An AI-generated reference summary presents this research as showing that exogenous testosterone speeds bench press gains.[2] Wikipedia lists drug use among the factors behind rising record lifts.[1]

Trials and meta-analyses cover split versus full-body routines,[7][8] training volume,[11] minimum effective dose,[12] rest intervals,[13] effort to failure,[15] protein,[17] creatine,[18] magnesium[19] and supraphysiologic testosterone.[20] A 2024 study in Frontiers in Physiology examined musculoskeletal shoulder loads across bench press technique variations and their potential injury risk.[21] Another trial examined shoulder proprioception after strength training.[16]

Wikipedia lists distal clavicular osteolysis, rotator cuff tears and pectoral tears among reported injuries, along with cervical disc problems, rare spinal cord injury, subclavian vein thrombosis and asphyxiation from being trapped under the bar; it cites a 2004 petition to the US Consumer Product Safety Commission reporting several deaths a year.[1] Dumbbells reduce some of these risks because they can be dropped to the side.[1] Technique variations load the shoulder differently according to a 2024 biomechanical study.[21]

Commonly cited precautions include progressive loading, spotters or safety bars, rotator-cuff and scapular stability work, and coaching for beginners; an AI-generated reference summary also criticises ego lifting, meaning heavy attempts with poor form.[2]

On looksmax.org the bench press features as a strength benchmark. Members post milestones such as reaching two 45-lb plates a side on incline bench,[4] ask others for their one-rep maxes,[5] and joke about gym culture, including a thread on a lifter playing popular TikTok audio before his set.[22] Replies to milestone posts are mixed, ranging from teasing about small numbers to encouragement from beginners.[4] Forum discussion generally treats chest and shoulder size as part of an overall physique that members compare, rather than the bench number itself.

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing and lifting forums the bench press is discussed as a measure of progress and as a way to build chest and shoulder size, with members sharing numbers and debating whether heavy pressing or lighter, higher-rep work builds the better-looking physique.[4][5][9]

claims.claim: The bench press is the best way to build a bigger chest.
Hitting a number such as the 225 club marks a real standard of physique progress.
Supplements like creatine and protein raise bench press numbers and lean mass.
Dropping the barbell bench in favour of other lifts is fine for chest development.
Heavy benching carries a meaningful injury risk to the shoulder and chest.

timeline.event: George Hackenschmidt performs a strict floor press of 164 kg.[1]
Joe Nordquest beats the floor press mark by 1 kg.[1]
The bench press becomes the standard chest exercise, overtaking the parallel dip.[1]
The International Powerlifting Federation is founded, according to an AI-generated reference summary.[2]
NEJM trial reports that supraphysiologic testosterone increases muscle size and strength in normal men.[20]
Julius Maddox sets the cited raw record of 355 kg on 21 February.[2]
